item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: If you want to go the historical route, there's always pitch cards. Circuses used to sell them as little souvenirs to visitors as a way to remind them of what they saw. One side of the card would have a photograph or illustration of a performer, and the other side would often have short biography.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: This was my thinking of what HF's format would be; receipts, invoices, etc. The posters have obvious visual appeal, yes, but they do heavily limit your room for exposition. Limiting can be good, a la 173, but forced limiting too far will restrict the complexity (and therefore interest) of what future creators can do with the concept.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: I have a suggestion about that, actually. The circus might not have any particular reason to keep detailed documentation about its acts, that's true, but every establishment of this size and complexity will likely need some sort of paperwork for other, seemingly mundane reasons: payment records for the performs, logistical accounts by the stage crews, scripts for the shows, even stuff like vendor orders (the flaming man's daily supply of coal, things on that line). You'd be surprised how much documents like this can reveal about an organization, and what a story they can tell; indeed, it's often those documents that historians prize most when researching something. I think you can get a lot of interesting information to the reader using such methods.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
What I think hits us hardest in this contest is the fact that while in-universe there's little reason for Fuller to keep more documentation on his employees than their name and what to pay them, the reader base still expects full disclosure on who they are, where they came from. The format we currently have limits us in that, really limits us in that. I personally think that from the GoI's perspective, this format makes the most sense, but I can see that in addition to being immersive, it also has to address the expectations of its audience.

We're on it.
